questions.prompt: How many possible configurations does a system of n classical bits have, and how many of those configurations is the system actually in at any given instant?
options: 2^n possible configurations, but exactly one at any instant
2^n possible configurations, and all of them simultaneously
n possible configurations, one at a time
2^n configurations, n of which are active at once
questions.explain: n classical bits have a state space of 2^n distinct configurations, but the physical system always occupies exactly one of those configurations at a time — the exponential number counts possibilities, not simultaneous occupation. This is the exact contrast point the course uses to introduce the qubit's genuinely different behavior.

questions.prompt: A qubit is prepared as |ψ⟩ = (1/√2)|0⟩ + (1/√2)|1⟩. Select all statements that are true about this state.
options: Measuring this qubit gives outcome 0 with probability 0.5 and outcome 1 with probability 0.5
The qubit is physically in both the 0 and 1 state at once before measurement
The two amplitudes are equal, each with magnitude 1/√2
After measurement, the qubit collapses to exactly one of |0⟩ or |1⟩
questions.explain: The Born rule gives P(0)=P(1)=|1/√2|²=0.5, and the two amplitudes are indeed equal. Measurement causes collapse to a single definite outcome. The 'both 0 and 1 at once' framing is the pop-science myth the lesson explicitly rejects — superposition is a precise statement about a well-defined vector, not simultaneous occupation of two classical states.

questions.prompt: For a 3-qubit uniform superposition where every one of the 8 amplitudes equals 1/√8, what is the measurement probability of any single one of the 8 basis outcomes? Express as a decimal.
questions.explain: Each probability is |1/√8|² = 1/8 = 0.125, and the lesson confirmed via node that 8 × 0.125 sums to 1 (up to floating-point rounding) — exactly the Born rule applied to a uniform 3-qubit superposition.

questions.prompt: A colleague claims that putting 20 qubits into a uniform superposition lets a quantum computer 'check all 1,048,576 answers simultaneously and just read off the right one' with no further work. What is the specific flaw in this claim?
options: Measuring the system yields exactly one randomly sampled 20-bit string according to the Born rule; without first using interference to concentrate probability on the correct answer, that one sample is no more useful than a random guess
20 qubits cannot actually be placed into a uniform superposition
A uniform superposition only has 20 amplitudes, not 2^20
Measurement would reveal all 1,048,576 amplitudes directly
questions.explain: The course is explicit that superposition alone gives zero computational advantage at readout time — a single measurement only yields one classical sample, and a uniform superposition samples uniformly at random. Real speedups require interference to amplify the correct answer's amplitude before measurement.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguish real quantum speedups (as covered in this course) from the 'tries everything at once for free' myth? Select all that apply.
options: Shor's and Grover's algorithms each exploit a specific mathematical structure in their problem, rather than being generic superposition tricks
Grover's algorithm gives only a quadratic (√N), not exponential, speedup, and is provably optimal for unstructured search
Every quantum algorithm automatically achieves an exponential speedup over the best classical algorithm for the same problem
A useful quantum algorithm must be engineered so that interference concentrates probability on the correct answer before the single measurement collapses the state
questions.explain: Shor's algorithm exploits periodicity via the quantum Fourier transform; Grover's gives a quadratic, provably optimal speedup for unstructured search — neither is a generic 'add more qubits' trick, and there is no universal exponential speedup for arbitrary problems.

questions.prompt: Which 2x2 matrix correctly represents the Hadamard gate H?
questions.explain: H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,-1]] is the Hadamard matrix. The other options are, respectively, the Pauli X, Pauli Z, and S gate matrices — each a different, fixed single-qubit gate covered in this chapter.

questions.prompt: The lesson applies Z to the superposition (1/√2)|0⟩ + (1/√2)|1⟩, producing (1/√2)|0⟩ − (1/√2)|1⟩. Select all true statements about this result.
options: The measurement probabilities before and after applying Z are both exactly 0.5/0.5
The sign flip on the |1⟩ term is a relative phase, invisible to a direct measurement in the computational basis alone
Because the probabilities didn't change, the state vector before and after Z are actually identical
This relative phase becomes observable once the qubit passes through an interference-capable gate afterward
questions.explain: Z changes the state vector (a sign flips) but not the measurement probabilities, since squaring removes the sign. This relative phase is invisible to a lone measurement but becomes observable once combined with an interference step like another Hadamard — which is exactly why Z is almost always paired with H in real circuits.

questions.prompt: The T gate satisfies T^n = I for the smallest positive integer n. What is that value of n?
questions.explain: T applies a 45° phase step, so 8 applications bring the phase all the way around the unit circle back to the start: T⁸ = I. This is why T is called an 'eighth-turn' gate, distinguishing it from the 'quarter-turn' S and 'half-turn' Z.

questions.prompt: Ry(π/2) applied to |0⟩ gives (1/√2, 1/√2), numerically identical to H|0⟩. A student concludes Ry(π/2) and H must be the same gate. What's the correct way to evaluate this claim, and what's the actual answer?
options: Check both basis vectors, not just one — Ry(π/2)|1⟩ gives (−1/√2, 1/√2), the negative of H|1⟩ = (1/√2, −1/√2), so the two gates are related but not identical
The claim is correct, since matching on |0⟩ is sufficient to prove two single-qubit gates are identical
The claim is correct because all single-qubit rotation gates are mathematically identical to H
The claim is false because Ry(π/2) cannot be applied to |0⟩ at all
questions.explain: Two gates agreeing on one basis vector's output does not mean they are the same gate — the full matrix (or at minimum both basis vectors) must be checked. Ry(π/2) and H agree on |0⟩ but differ by a sign on |1⟩, making them related but genuinely distinct gates.

questions.prompt: Regarding gate order and phase (from the Single-Qubit Gates Problem-Solving Lab's X-then-Z vs. Z-then-X comparison), select all true statements.
options: Applying X then Z to |0⟩ gives −|1⟩, while applying Z then X to |0⟩ gives |1⟩ — these are different vectors, showing X and Z do not commute
Because the difference between the two orders in that specific example was only an overall sign, it is always safe to assume gate order never matters
A relative phase introduced by swapping gate order can change downstream measurement probabilities once another interfering gate is applied
The correct discipline is to compute each gate sequence explicitly rather than assume gates commute
questions.explain: X and Z do not commute (XZ = −ZX), confirmed numerically. The lesson explicitly warns against over-generalizing from this one case — a phase difference from reordering gates is not always a harmless global phase, and must be checked directly on a superposition, not assumed.

questions.prompt: Regarding the CNOT gate, select all true statements.
options: CNOT flips the target qubit if and only if the control qubit is |1⟩
CNOT is equivalent to applying X independently to both qubits (X⊗X)
CNOT squared equals the identity matrix
CNOT applied to any single computational basis state always produces another single basis state, never a superposition
questions.explain: CNOT conditionally flips only the target, unlike X⊗X which unconditionally flips both qubits — they give different results on |10⟩. CNOT is its own inverse, and feeding it a basis state always yields another basis state; entanglement only appears when CNOT acts on a superposition.

questions.prompt: A reversed CNOT (control=q2, target=q1) is applied to the Bell state (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2. A student assumes this leaves the state unchanged because the state 'looks symmetric' in its two qubits. What does the actual computation show?
options: The reversed CNOT produces (|00⟩+|01⟩)/√2, a genuinely different state — the symmetric appearance of the original state does not make it a fixed point of the reversed gate
The state is indeed left unchanged, confirming the student's intuition
The reversed CNOT destroys the state entirely, leaving all zero amplitudes
The reversed CNOT produces (|10⟩+|01⟩)/√2
questions.explain: The reversed CNOT flips q1 whenever q2 is |1⟩, turning the |11⟩ term into |01⟩ while leaving |00⟩ alone, giving (|00⟩+|01⟩)/√2. The lab's point is precisely that this 'intuitive' symmetry guess is wrong, and only direct computation catches it.

questions.prompt: Starting from |00⟩, applying H to qubit 1 then CNOT(control=q1,target=q2) produces the Bell state with state vector [0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071] in the |00⟩,|01⟩,|10⟩,|11⟩ basis. What is the measurement probability (as a decimal) of observing outcome |01⟩ for this state?
questions.explain: The amplitude at the |01⟩ position is exactly 0, so its measurement probability is 0² = 0. Only |00⟩ and |11⟩ have nonzero probability (0.5 each), which is the perfect-correlation signature of entanglement.

questions.prompt: Regarding the Toffoli (CCNOT) gate, select all true statements.
options: Toffoli flips its target qubit if and only if both of its two control qubits are |1⟩
Toffoli can compute classical AND logic into the target qubit (when the target starts at |0⟩) while remaining fully reversible
Toffoli can be built directly from single-qubit gates and CNOT alone, with no extra ancilla qubits needed
Toffoli is its own inverse, since applying it twice returns the system to its original state
questions.explain: Toffoli swaps |110⟩↔|111⟩ and leaves everything else fixed, giving reversible AND logic. The lesson is explicit that Toffoli genuinely needs ancilla qubits and a longer gate sequence to build from single- and two-qubit gates — it cannot be done with CNOT alone.

questions.prompt: CZ (controlled-Z) is applied to the uniform 2-qubit superposition (|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩+|11⟩)/2, giving (|00⟩+|01⟩+|10⟩−|11⟩)/2. Why does this NOT change any measurement probability, yet is still considered a physically meaningful change to the state?
options: Squaring −1 and +1 both give 1, so the probabilities (1/4 each) are unchanged, but the sign flip is a relative phase specific to the |11⟩ term that becomes observable through later interference, unlike a phase applied uniformly to the whole vector
The probabilities did change, from 1/4 each to 1/3 each
CZ only affects amplitudes, which have no physical meaning independent of probabilities under any circumstance
The sign flip is a global phase, identical in effect to multiplying the entire state vector by −1
questions.explain: A phase on one term out of a superposition (relative phase) is physically meaningful in a way a phase on the whole vector (global phase) never is — it leaves probabilities unchanged here but would show up in any interference experiment recombining the terms.

questions.prompt: In standard quantum circuit diagram notation, select all true statements.
options: Time flows left to right along each qubit's wire
A filled dot connected by a vertical line to a ⊕ symbol represents a controlled operation like CNOT
A double line following a measurement symbol represents a second qubit, not a classical bit
A box labeled with a gate name on a wire means that gate is applied to that qubit at that point in time
questions.explain: A double line after a measurement represents a classical bit carrying the measurement outcome, not a second qubit — this distinction matters directly for reading the teleportation circuit, where classical bits must physically travel to Bob.

questions.prompt: A 3-qubit circuit applies H to qubit 1 and H to qubit 2 in the same layer, then applies CNOT with control=q1, target=q2; qubit 3 has no gates. What are this circuit's width and depth?
options: Width 3, depth 2
Width 2, depth 2
Width 3, depth 3
Width 3, depth 1
questions.explain: Width counts all qubits in the register (3), regardless of whether every qubit has a gate. The two H gates act on disjoint qubits and share layer 1; the CNOT depends on both post-H qubits so it must be layer 2 — depth 2 total.

questions.prompt: This course's standard universal gate set is {H, T, ___}. Name the missing two-qubit gate.
questions.explain: {H, T, CNOT} is the standard universal gate set: H and T together can approximate any single-qubit rotation to arbitrary precision, and CNOT supplies all the entangling power any circuit needs.

questions.prompt: Regarding the verified fact that S = T² (shown by direct complex matrix multiplication), select all true statements.
options: T applied twice in sequence reproduces the S gate exactly, with no approximation error
Since S² = Z, it follows that T⁴ = Z
Since T⁴ = Z, applying T eight times reproduces the identity gate, T⁸ = I
This decomposition proves S cannot be part of any universal gate set
questions.explain: T² = S exactly (verified by complex matrix multiplication), so T⁴ = (T²)² = S² = Z, and T⁸ = (T⁴)² = Z² = I. This chain is exactly why T is called an 'eighth-turn' gate and is central to universal gate sets, not evidence against them.

questions.prompt: A circuit is designed to turn |00⟩ into (|00⟩ − |11⟩)/√2 using H on qubit 1, then Z on qubit 1, then CNOT(control=q1,target=q2). What verified role does the Z gate play in this specific sequence?
options: Applied right after H and before CNOT, Z flips the sign specifically on the component where qubit 1 is |1⟩ (the |10⟩ term), and CNOT then carries that sign through to land specifically on the final |11⟩ term
Z has no effect at all in this position and was included only for symmetry
Z converts the circuit's output into a non-normalized state
Z changes the measurement probabilities of the final state relative to the standard Bell state
questions.explain: The lesson traced this step by step: H gives (|00⟩+|10⟩)/√2, Z gives (|00⟩−|10⟩)/√2 (sign only on the q1=1 term), and CNOT moves that sign onto |11⟩, producing exactly (|00⟩−|11⟩)/√2 — the target specification, verified numerically rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: Regarding the quantum teleportation protocol, select all true statements.
options: Alice needs to know the amplitudes a and b of the state |ψ⟩ she is teleporting
Alice's two classical measurement bits must physically reach Bob before he can recover |ψ⟩
The protocol requires a pre-shared Bell pair distributed before Alice has her unknown state
Alice's original qubit still holds |ψ⟩ after she measures it
questions.explain: Alice never learns a and b — the protocol works precisely because she doesn't need to. The Bell pair must be pre-shared, and Bob genuinely needs Alice's classical bits to select the right correction; her original qubit is destroyed (collapsed) by her own measurement.

questions.prompt: In the verified teleportation trace with |ψ⟩ = 0.8|0⟩ + 0.6|1⟩, Alice measures outcome '01' and Bob's raw (unnormalized) qubit amplitudes are (0.3, 0.4), normalizing to (0.6, 0.8). What correction must Bob apply to recover |ψ⟩ = (0.8, 0.6), and why does it work?
options: Apply X, which swaps the two amplitudes, turning (0.6, 0.8) into (0.8, 0.6) = |ψ⟩
Apply Z, which flips the sign of the second amplitude, giving (0.6, -0.8)
Apply nothing (I), since (0.6, 0.8) already equals |ψ⟩
Apply Z then X, giving (-0.8, 0.6)
questions.explain: The '01' outcome leaves Bob's qubit with the amplitudes swapped relative to |ψ⟩. X is exactly the gate that swaps a qubit's two amplitudes, correctly restoring (0.8, 0.6) — matching the standard 00→I, 01→X, 10→Z, 11→XZ correction table verified with real numbers in the lesson.

questions.prompt: In superdense coding, Alice encodes 2 classical bits by applying one gate to her own qubit, then physically sends only that one qubit to Bob. How many classical bits of information does Bob recover from this single physically-transmitted qubit (combined with the pre-shared entangled pair)?
questions.explain: Bob recovers exactly 2 classical bits from the 1 physically transmitted qubit — double the usual 1-bit-per-qubit classical limit, made possible by the pre-shared entangled pair (the protocol's 'hidden cost').

questions.prompt: Regarding why teleportation and superdense coding do not violate the no-cloning theorem or special relativity, select all true statements.
options: Teleportation never has two independent copies of |ψ⟩ coexisting — the original is destroyed by measurement before Bob's qubit becomes usable as |ψ⟩
Superdense coding is never at risk of violating no-cloning because Alice only ever manipulates a known, classical choice of gate, not an unknown state
Bob's qubit, before Alice's classical bits arrive, is indistinguishable from a maximally mixed/informationless state, so no faster-than-light signal has occurred
Because Alice's measurement instantly determines which of 4 states Bob's qubit is in, information has traveled to Bob faster than light
questions.explain: Teleportation performs destruction-then-recreation, never duplication, so no-cloning never applies. Superdense coding never attempts to copy an unknown state at all. And Bob's qubit looks informationless until the classical bits physically arrive — no signal travels faster than that classical channel allows.

questions.prompt: In the superdense coding diagnostic exercise, Alice encodes '10' with Z, Bob correctly applies CNOT(q1→q2), but forgets the final H gate before measuring. What actually happens?
options: Bob measures '00' or '10' at random with 50/50 probability, never '01' or '11' — the second bit is permanently lost and the first bit becomes a coin flip instead of a deterministic '1'
Bob still recovers '10' correctly, since CNOT alone is sufficient to decode the message
Bob measures '11' with certainty
Bob's measurement becomes completely unpredictable across all four possible 2-bit outcomes
questions.explain: Skipping H leaves the state at [0.7071, 0, -0.7071, 0], giving exactly 0.5 probability each to |00⟩ and |10⟩ and zero to the others — both decode gates are load-bearing, and dropping either one destroys the deterministic readout entirely rather than merely degrading it.

questions.prompt: Regarding how a classical simulator represents and evolves a quantum state, select all true statements.
options: An n-qubit state is stored as an array of 2^n complex amplitudes
A single-qubit gate can be applied to one qubit in a larger system by pairing up basis-state indices that differ only in that qubit's bit, without building the full 2^n × 2^n matrix
Applying a gate to qubit k always requires constructing and storing the entire 2^n × 2^n matrix first
The Born rule (squaring each amplitude's magnitude) gives the exact measurement probability for each basis state in a simulator
questions.explain: The index-pairing technique is precisely what avoids ever building the full exponentially large gate matrix — it only touches the fixed 2x2 gate and pairs of array entries, which is how real simulators like Qiskit's Aer apply gates efficiently.

questions.prompt: Using the formula 2^n × 16 bytes for a full-precision state vector, how many gigabytes of memory does a 30-qubit simulation require? (give a whole number)
questions.explain: 2^30 × 16 bytes = 17,179,869,184 bytes = exactly 16 GB, as confirmed by the real node-computed table in the lesson — right at the edge of what a high-end consumer machine can hold.

questions.prompt: A real 1,000-shot simulation of a Bell-state measurement (true probabilities exactly 0.5/0/0/0.5) produced actual counts of 487/0/0/513 rather than exactly 500/0/0/500. What does this best illustrate about real quantum hardware?
options: Real hardware can only be measured once per run and collapses the state, so probabilities must be estimated from finite repeated shots, which only approximate (not exactly match) the true probabilities
The true probabilities must actually be 0.487 and 0.513, not 0.5 and 0.5
This indicates a bug in the Born rule itself
Real hardware always produces exactly the predicted probabilities for any number of shots
questions.explain: A simulator can print exact probabilities directly from the state vector; real hardware can only estimate them by running the full circuit many times and tallying outcomes, which is why finite shot counts show ordinary statistical fluctuation around the true probability rather than matching it exactly.

questions.prompt: Regarding the exponential wall and why real quantum hardware avoids it, select all true statements.
options: A classical simulator's memory requirement doubles with every additional qubit, since it must store 2^n amplitudes
A real quantum computer with n physical qubits must also explicitly store 2^n numbers somewhere to represent its own state
Around n=40-50 qubits, full-precision classical simulation becomes infeasible even on the largest supercomputers
The index-pairing technique for applying gates efficiently also reduces the total size of the state vector that must be stored
questions.explain: A real quantum computer's n qubits simply are in their joint state as a physical fact, with no explicit 2^n-number storage needed — unlike a classical simulator. Index-pairing makes gate application efficient but cannot shrink the state vector itself, since a general n-qubit state genuinely has 2^n independent amplitudes.

questions.prompt: The capstone simulator core's GATES object includes H, X, and Z, all implemented with real-valued matrix entries, and applySingleQubitGate works correctly for all three. Why would adding the S gate (matrix [[1,0],[0,i]]) to this same object, unchanged, produce incorrect results?
options: The core's state array and gate-application function only handle real numbers; S's matrix entry i is imaginary, so correctly supporting it requires changing the state representation to track real and imaginary parts, not just adding a new matrix
S cannot be represented as a 2x2 matrix at all
applySingleQubitGate only supports exactly 3-qubit systems
The GATES object in JavaScript cannot hold more than three entries
questions.explain: H, X, and Z all happen to have purely real matrix entries, which is why this deliberately minimal capstone core handles them correctly. S (like Y and the rotation gates) needs genuine complex arithmetic, which is exactly the gap between this hand-built core and a production simulator.
